Title: Compact Scheduler and Eviction De-escalation Notes
Content:
Summary / motivation
We have a mature KV cache design with per-tenant partitions, slab-like pools and a set of eviction/compaction heuristics. Operational telemetry shows two recurring pain points in 1P and Dedicated runs:
- Frequent short-lived, high-priority evictions (hard-evict) triggered by sudden memory pressure spikes that cause throughput spikes and tail-latency regressions.
- Background compaction/defrag passes that either run too aggressively (stealing cycles from inference) or too infrequently (allowing fragmentation to accumulate), and no clear coordination between compaction and eviction.

This note sketches a design for a Compact Scheduler and an Eviction De-escalation protocol aimed at reducing unnecessary hard-evictions, smoothing latency tail events, and improving long-term fragmentation behavior without compromising memory safety or tenant isolation.

Goals
- Reduce hard-eviction events by introducing graded de-escalation steps before reclamation.
- Coordinate compaction and eviction work via a scheduler that understands QoS budgets, tenant priorities, and machine load.
- Provide knobs that let SRE/product tune safety vs cost tradeoffs: e.g., aggressive compaction windows for batch-only clusters, conservative de-escalation for strict latency SLOs.
- Produce telemetry for debugging and automated policies (SLO-aware autoscaling, adaptive compaction pacing).

Constraints and invariants
- Under no circumstance should the scheduler produce conditions that allow token generation or model state corruption; memory bounds must be maintained.
- Tenant isolation must be preserved: de-escalation should not cause a tenant to exceed its hard memory cap.
- Any background compaction must be preemptible and yield to inference threads in the critical path.
- Changes must be incrementally deployable; fallback to current hard-evict-only behavior must be simple.

Design overview
We introduce two primary components:
1) Compact Scheduler: a lightweight controller that maintains a queue of candidates (fragments, cold slots, micro-slab gaps) and schedules background compaction tasks with a paced budget.
2) Eviction De-escalator: a fast-path policy layer that replaces immediate hard-evict decisions with a graded set of remedial actions (soft demotion, async compaction request, tenant-refill-delay, spill-to-disk attempt) until a hard-evict remains necessary.

Key concepts
- QoS Budget (QB): per-machine and per-tenant budgets expressed as CPU-ms/sec and IO-ms/sec that background tasks can consume. QB enforces that compaction cannot starve inference.
- De-escalation Ladder: sequence of steps attempted before hard-evict. Examples: 1) try reclaiming free micro-slots in same arena; 2) request in-place defragmentation of nearby slots; 3) prioritize compacting other less-latent tenants with spare QB; 4) attempt spill-to-disk for cold keys (if configured); 5) final hard-evict.
- Fragment Score: probabilistic metric for each region that combines occupancy, fragmentation ratio, and access hotness to prioritize compaction.
- Compact Windows: small time windows (configurable, e.g., 10-200ms) where a compaction worker will acquire a region and attempt limited merges/pulls before releasing.

Compact Scheduler details
- Input streams:
  - periodic sampler produces Fragment Score candidates for compaction
  - reclamation requests (triggered by De-escalator)
  - telemetry-driven triggers (heatmap shows growing fragmentation)
- Priority queue keyed by (tenant_priority, fragment_score, estimated_compact_cost)
- Worker model: a pool of N background compaction workers per machine; each worker consumes QB; workers run cooperative compaction in preemptible micro-windows to avoid stalling inference threads.
- Cost estimation: approximate CPU and wall-time cost for a compact operation derived from region size and expected moves. Conservative estimates used for scheduling; adaptive learning hooks added to refine estimates over time (see linked_artifacts PR/metrics).
- Local thrift: when a worker cannot acquire QB from local tenant, it will attempt to barter capacity by compacting low-priority fragments for other tenants that have surplus QB (helps knock down global fragmentation without hurting top-tier tenants).

Eviction De-escalation flow
When a request would trigger a hard-eviction (memory pressure detected):
1) Fast-path checks: if free reservation > threshold, do normal admission.
2) If below threshold, De-escalator runs the ladder in order. Each step is time-boxed so request latency does not exceed configured SLO slack (e.g., 2-5ms extra allowed for soft remediation).
3) Steps:
   - Local micro-reclaim: scan the same arena for tiny free slots or tombstones that can be reclaimed synchronously (cheap). If successful, proceed with request.
   - Async compact hint: attach a high-priority compaction request to the scheduler for the region and proceed while the request waits on a short retry backoff (client will be offered an early retry policy). This reduces immediate eviction while compaction happens.
   - Tenant backpressure: if tenant has refill/burst credits, slow admission for low-priority requests (e.g., prefetches, background warmups) to reduce memory churn.
   - Spill attempt: if on-prem/private set up with configured spill, attempt controlled spill of cold pages to local SSD; this is higher IO cost and must respect QB budget.
   - Hard-evict: only if previous steps fail or if immediate memory reclaim is necessary to preserve safety.

Memory Pools and fragmentation handling
- Pools: we keep existing per-tenant pool + global cold pool. Compact Scheduler will sometimes migrate cold regions into the global cold pool to create larger contiguous free runs.
- Micro-slab coalescing: when free micro-slots adjacent and within same allocation unit, compact worker will coalesce to create larger runs, improving allocator efficiency.
- Aging-based promotion: short-lived allocations are kept in a fast churn pool; once an object survives N windows, it is promoted to the long-lived pool which is compacted less often.

Telemetry and observability
Expose the following metrics per-machine and per-tenant:
- compaction_cycles_used (CPU-ms)
- compaction_windows_triggered
- compaction_success_rate (reclaimed bytes / attempted bytes)
- deescalation_attempts_by_step (counts of each ladder step)
- hard_evictions (counter)
- fragmentation_ratio_by_region
- QB_consumed_by_tenant
- avg_compact_latency

Spans/events to log (for traces):
- deescalation path taken with timings
- compaction candidate selection reason and estimate
- worker preemption events (when compaction yielded to inference)

Configuration knobs (initial suggestion)
- qb.cpu_ms_per_sec (machine-level)
- qb.io_ms_per_sec
- deescalation.max_extra_latency_ms (SLO slack allowed)
- deescalation.ladder_enabled_steps (bitmask)
- compact.worker_count
- compact.window_ms_min, compact.window_ms_max
- compact.estimate_overhead_factor (safety multiplier)
- pool.promotion_threshold_windows
- spill.enabled, spill.max_write_mb_per_sec

Safety, fallback, and rollout plan
- Start with a read-only telemetry-only rollout: enable scheduler with qb=0, log candidate selections and de-escalation decisions without changing behavior.
- Next, enable async compaction requests but do not disable hard-evict. Observe compaction_success_rate and effect on hard_evictions.
- Enable QB with conservative CPU budget (1-2% CPU) and run A/B against control clusters for 2 weeks.
- If stable, gradually increase QB and enable tenant barter and spill in controlled clusters.
- Always provide a feature flag to revert to hard-evict-only at the machine level.

Experiments to run
- Controlled burst test: synthetic workload that creates a 20% memory pressure spike for 60s; measure difference in hard-evictions and tail latency with/without de-escalation.
- Fragmentation regression: create churn-heavy tiny-allocation workload and measure fragmentation_ratio over time with compact windows tuned low vs high.
- Tenant-mix fairness: run mixed-priority tenants and test barter behavior to ensure high-priority tenants maintain latency SLOs.

Open questions / discussion items
- Spill semantics: do we prefer SSD spill or networked object storage for private deployments? Latency/IO reliability tradeoffs need infra input.
- QB accounting: should QB budgets be transferable across machines in a rack when local QB is exhausted? Complexity vs benefit tradeoff.
- Learning-based cost estimates: prototyping an online RL learner may improve scheduling but adds system complexity; initial rollout should use heuristics.
- Backpressure policies for clients: what is the suggested client retry/backoff integration surface? Should SDKs expose a "de-escalation-retry" header to avoid duplicate tokens? Engineering to coordinate with SDK team.

Appendix: quick algorithm sketches
- Fragment Score = alpha*(1 - occupancy_ratio) + beta*fragmentation_ratio + gamma*(1 - normalized_hotness)
- De-escalation step timeouts: arithmetic backoff: t_n = base_ms * (2^n) but clipped to deescalation.max_extra_latency_ms

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally a middle-level design doc; please focus feedback on XBQ accounting model, compaction window sizing and safety invariants. Link implementation concerns/PRs to JIRA-RT-982 and the prototype PR in linked artifacts.
